Maximal coverage location-allocation

Source: R/allocation.R
allocation.Rd

allocation() and allocation_discrete() allocate new facilities so as to maximize the share of (optionally weighted) demand that can reach a facility within objectiveminutes minutes.

  • allocation() solves a continuous problem: new facilities can be placed anywhere within bb_area (any cell of the demand grid).

  • allocation_discrete() solves a discrete problem: new facilities are selected from a user-defined set of candidate locations.

Both functions can either add facilities until a target coverage (objectiveshare) is reached, using as few facilities as possible, or allocate a fixed maximum number of facilities (n_fac).

Usage

allocation(
  demand,
  bb_area,
  facilities,
  traveltime = NULL,
  mode = "walk",
  dowscaling_model_type = NULL,
  res_output = 100,
  weights = NULL,
  objectiveminutes = 15,
  objectiveshare = 0.99,
  heur = "kd",
  approach = "norm",
  exp_demand = 1,
  exp_weights = 1,
  n_fac = Inf,
  shortlist = 10,
  refine = TRUE
)

allocation_discrete(
  demand,
  bb_area,
  candidate,
  facilities = NULL,
  n_fac = Inf,
  n_samples,
  traveltime = NULL,
  mode = "walk",
  dowscaling_model_type = NULL,
  res_output = 100,
  weights = NULL,
  objectiveminutes = 15,
  objectiveshare = NULL,
  approach = "norm",
  exp_demand = 1,
  exp_weights = 1,
  par = FALSE
)

Arguments

demand

A RasterLayer or single-layer SpatRaster object with the demand (e.g., number of people per cell), in geographic coordinates (WGS 84). It defines the grid of the analysis.

bb_area

A sf object with the polygon(s) of the area of interest.

facilities

A sf object with the existing facilities, or NULL if there are no existing facilities. Required by allocation() (use facilities = NULL explicitly to allocate from scratch); optional in allocation_discrete() (default: NULL).

traveltime

(optional) The output of the traveltime() function, whose friction surface is reused to avoid downloading and downscaling it again. The travel times from facilities are recomputed on this surface. If NULL, the friction surface is computed with friction() using mode and res_output (default: NULL).

mode

(optional) A character string indicating the mode of transport. Options are "fastest" and "walk" (default: "walk").

  • For "fastest": The friction layer accounts for multiple modes of transport, including walking and driving. At the native resolution, it is the Malaria Atlas Project (2015) Global Travel Speed Friction Surface.

  • For "walk": The friction layer accounts only for walking speeds and is based on the Malaria Atlas Project (2020) Global Walking Only Friction Surface.

dowscaling_model_type

Deprecated and ignored. The friction surface is no longer downscaled with a statistical model (see Details).

res_output

(optional) A positive integerish number indicating the spatial resolution of the friction raster (and of the analysis), in meters. See Details (default: 100).

weights

(optional) A RasterLayer or SpatRaster object with the weights for the demand (e.g., a hazard layer). It is resampled to the grid of demand if needed (default: NULL).

objectiveminutes

(optional) A number indicating the travel time threshold, in minutes, within which demand is considered covered (default: 15).

objectiveshare

(optional) A number between 0 and 1 indicating the share of the (weighted) demand to be covered. In allocation() it can only be NULL if n_fac is finite (default: 0.99 for allocation() and NULL for allocation_discrete()).

heur

(optional) The score used by allocation() to shortlist promising locations for each new facility. Options are "kd" and "max". See Details (default: "kd").

approach

(optional) The approach used to combine the demand and weights layers. Options are "norm" and "absweights". See Details (default: "norm").

exp_demand

(optional) The exponent applied to the demand layer. Values greater than 1 increase the relative priority of high-demand cells, and the influence of demand with respect to weights (default: 1).

exp_weights

(optional) The exponent applied to the weights layer. Values greater than 1 increase the relative priority of cells with high weights, and the influence of weights with respect to demand (default: 1).

n_fac

(optional) A positive integerish number indicating the maximum number of new facilities to allocate. In allocation_discrete(), it is capped at the number of candidate locations (default: Inf).

shortlist

(optional) A positive integerish number indicating how many new promising locations allocation() evaluates exactly at each iteration. See Details (default: 10).

refine

(optional) A logical flag indicating whether allocation() refines the greedy solution by vertex substitution (see Details). Refinement usually reduces the number of facilities needed for a given coverage, but takes more time (default: TRUE).

candidate

A sf object with the candidate locations (POINT geometries) for the new facilities (allocation_discrete() only).

n_samples

Deprecated and ignored. allocation_discrete() no longer relies on random sampling (allocation_discrete() only).

par

(optional) A logical flag indicating whether to compute the travel times from the candidate locations in parallel (allocation_discrete() only; default: FALSE).

Value

An invisible list of class allocation (continuous problem) or allocation_discrete (discrete problem) with the following elements:

  • coverage: A numeric value indicating the share of (weighted) demand covered within the objective travel time after allocating the new facilities.

  • unmet_demand: A numeric value indicating the share of (weighted) demand that remains unmet after allocating the new facilities.

  • objective_minutes: The value of the objectiveminutes parameter used.

  • objective_share: The value of the objectiveshare parameter used.

  • facilities: A sf object with the newly allocated facilities (for allocation_discrete(), the selected rows of candidate).

  • travel_time: A RasterLayer object, on the grid of demand, with the travel time (in minutes) to the nearest facility after allocating the new facilities.

Details

Coverage

A demand cell is covered when its travel time to the nearest (existing or new) facility is less than or equal to objectiveminutes. Coverage is the share of the total (weighted) demand within bb_area that is covered. Travel times are computed with the accumulated cost algorithm (gdistance::accCost()) over the friction surface and aligned to the grid of demand.

Continuous problem (allocation())

Facilities are added one at a time with a (lazy) greedy heuristic. At each iteration:

  1. A score of the demand not yet covered proposes a shortlist of promising locations: the shortlist highest local maxima of the score, at least half a catchment radius apart. The catchment radius is the distance that can be traveled within objectiveminutes at the median friction of the study area. The score is:

    • heur = "kd": the uncovered demand smoothed with a quartic kernel whose bandwidth is the catchment radius, i.e., an estimate of the uncovered demand within the catchment of a facility placed at each cell.

    • heur = "max": the uncovered demand of each cell.

  2. The catchment of each shortlisted location (the demand cells it can reach within objectiveminutes) is computed with the accumulated cost algorithm. Catchments do not change as facilities are added, so the locations evaluated in previous iterations remain candidates at no extra cost.

  3. The new facility is placed at the evaluated location that covers the largest amount of uncovered demand (greedy step of Church & ReVelle, 1974).

The greedy phase stops when objectiveshare is reached, when n_fac new facilities have been allocated, or when no further location increases the coverage. The solution is then refined (vertex substitution heuristic, Teitz & Bart, 1968): each facility is in turn moved to the evaluated location that covers the most demand left uncovered by the others, if that increases the coverage. New locations are evaluated near each facility at every pass: local maxima of the score, and eight locations around the facility at a distance that starts at half the catchment radius and is halved whenever the facility is not moved (pattern search). With objectiveshare, the facility covering the least demand on its own is then dropped and the solution refined again, as long as the target is still met.

Larger shortlist values evaluate more locations per iteration, which can yield better solutions at the cost of more travel time computations. Set refine = FALSE to skip the refinement phase for faster, greedy-only solutions.

Discrete problem (allocation_discrete())

Since the travel time from a set of facilities is the minimum of the travel times from each of them, the set of demand cells covered by each candidate location is computed once (one accumulated cost run per candidate). Then:

  1. Candidates are added one at a time, each time selecting the candidate that covers the largest amount of demand not yet covered (greedy heuristic, Church & ReVelle, 1974).

  2. The selection is refined by swapping selected and non-selected candidates as long as a swap increases the coverage (vertex substitution heuristic, Teitz & Bart, 1968).

If objectiveshare is NULL, up to n_fac candidates are selected to maximize coverage. Otherwise, candidates are added (and the selection refined) until objectiveshare is reached or n_fac candidates have been selected. The solution is deterministic and usually optimal or near-optimal.

Demand weights

When weights is provided, the demand to be covered is a combination of the demand and weights layers (e.g., population times exposure to a hazard):

  • approach = "norm": \(D^{a} \times W^{b}\), where \(D\) and \(W\) are the demand and weights layers rescaled to \([0, 1]\) (min-max normalization). Note that cells with the lowest weight receive zero priority.

  • approach = "absweights": \(D^{a} \times w^{b}\), where \(w\) are the raw (non-negative) weights. Priorities are proportional to the weights.

with \(a\) = exp_demand and \(b\) = exp_weights. Without weights, the demand is \(demand^{a}\). Coverage and objectiveshare then refer to this weighted demand.

References

Church, R., & ReVelle, C. (1974). The maximal covering location problem. Papers of the Regional Science Association, 32(1), 101–118. doi:10.1007/BF01942293

Teitz, M. B., & Bart, P. (1968). Heuristic methods for estimating the generalized vertex median of a weighted graph. Operations Research, 16(5), 955–961. doi:10.1287/opre.16.5.955

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
  library(sf)

  traveltime_data <-
    naples_fountains |>
    traveltime(bb_area = naples_shape)

  ## Continuous problem -----

  allocation_data <-
    naples_population |>
    allocation(
      bb_area = naples_shape,
      facilities = naples_fountains,
      traveltime = traveltime_data,
      weights = naples_hot_days,
      objectiveminutes = 15,
      objectiveshare = 0.99
    )

  allocation_data

  allocation_data |> allocation_plot(naples_shape)

  ## Discrete problem -----

  allocation_data <-
    naples_population |>
    allocation_discrete(
      bb_area = naples_shape,
      candidate = naples_shape |> st_sample(20),
      facilities = naples_fountains,
      traveltime = traveltime_data,
      n_fac = 2,
      objectiveminutes = 15
    )

  allocation_data

  allocation_data |> allocation_plot(naples_shape)
} # }
